item.title: Having a Baby on CrowdHealth: What $3,000 Covers
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: Pregnancy on CrowdHealth is one event with a $3,000 member commitment, if your due date is 300+ days after joining. What members say it's really like.
item.content:encoded:
In short: On CrowdHealth, a whole pregnancy is one health event with a $3,000 member commitment covering prenatal care, delivery, and postpartum. The catch is timing: your due date has to be at least 300 days after you join. Members report getting paid back in one to four weeks, and some say the billing paperwork felt like a part-time job.

Babies are the second biggest thing the CrowdHealth crowd pays for. The company expects about 800 of them this year. So there are a lot of member stories, and they rhyme.

What happened?

I pulled four recent ones.

A young family, members for almost two years, just had a baby. They pay around $250 to $300 a month and said the whole pregnancy was funded, usually within one to four weeks of turning in each bill. They said there was no haggling over any of it.

A mom expecting twins wrote that she'd already hit her $3,000 commitment, and everything she'd paid since had come back to her within weeks.

A third mom had a rougher ride. Pregnancy was her very first health event as a member. She had to collect itemized bills, talk to billing offices, pay up front, and wait to be paid back. She said it has still paid off compared to insurance. She also said the medical billing "felt like a part time job."

And a fourth, writing on her own blog, was using a birthing center. One of her larger bills sat unreviewed for about two months during a busy season. When she raised it, it was paid right away and she got an apology.

What does the bill look like?

Here's how the $3,000 works.

With regular health events, you pay the first $500. Pregnancy is different. It's one big event that covers everything from the first prenatal visit through postpartum, and your share is $3,000 total.

Think of it like a cover charge at a concert. You pay once at the door, and after that the show is covered, whether the band plays one set or three.

For comparison, a mom of three wrote that each of her earlier births on insurance cost her more than $6,000 out of pocket. And those were simple hospital births with no complications.

CrowdHealth says it also shares costs for midwives, doulas, lactation help, pelvic floor therapy, and one breast pump. About 40% of CrowdHealth babies are born at home and another 20% at birth centers.

What's the honest part?

There are three rules here that will bite you if you skip them.

The 300-day rule. Your due date has to be at least 300 days after your membership starts. If you're already pregnant when you join, that pregnancy isn't shared. This isn't something you sign up for after the test turns positive.

The price went up. Older reviews talk about having a baby for $500. That was true in 2022. It went to $1,500, and now it's $3,000. If you read an old review, check the date.

The baby is a separate person. Routine newborn care is its own event with its own $500. If the baby has complications at birth, that's another separate event. So a rough delivery could mean $3,000 plus $500 plus $500.

And you'll likely pay bills first and get paid back. That's a real cash flow thing to plan for.

The takeaway

For a planned pregnancy, $3,000 for the whole thing is a good deal next to what a lot of families pay on insurance. But it only works if you join well ahead of time and you're willing to keep your paperwork in order. Join first. Then plan the baby.

Yes, on the standard membership, if your due date is at least 300 days after you join. Your share is $3,000 for the whole pregnancy, including prenatal visits, delivery, and postpartum care. Pregnancies that started before you joined aren't shared. More in maternity on health sharing.

Yes. CrowdHealth lists certified midwives, doulas, birthing classes, and home birth supplies as eligible. Its founder says about 40% of member babies are born at home. Several members said choosing their own kind of birth was the reason they joined.

How long does it take to get paid back for pregnancy bills?

Members in public reviews report anywhere from a week to four weeks per bill. One blogger had a bill sit for about two months before it was fixed. Keep itemized bills and receipts, and plan to float some costs for a few weeks.

item.title: One Heart Procedure, Three Prices: $83,655, $44,000, and $22,000
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member was quoted $83,655, $44,000, and $22,000 for the same heart procedure. He paid $500 and 150 members funded the rest in 3 days.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A member needed a heart rhythm procedure. His local hospital quoted $83,655. A hospital 90 miles away quoted $44,000. One a few states away quoted $22,000. With travel, the whole thing came to about $30,000. He paid $500, and 150 members funded the other $29,500 in three days.

If I told you a gallon of milk cost $8 at one store and $2 at another, you'd drive. This is that, with a heart.

What happened?

CrowdHealth published this couple's story back in 2022. He's self-employed. His wife had lost her job, and the family's insurance went with it. They'd joined CrowdHealth a few months earlier and weren't sure yet that a crowd of strangers would really show up.

Then one day, mid-workout, his heart rate shot up to about 230 beats a minute and wouldn't come back down. The ER figured out what it was: a fast heart rhythm problem. The fix is a procedure where a doctor goes in and corrects the spot causing the trouble.

It worked. He was cleared with no restrictions afterward.

What did the bill look like?

This is the part that made my jaw drop. Same procedure, three hospitals:

  • Local hospital: $83,655
  • A big-city hospital about 90 miles away: $44,000
  • A hospital a few states away: $22,000

That's not a typo. The far one was about a quarter of the local one.

So they went. Plane tickets, three hotel nights, a driver, meals, and the procedure came to about $30,000 all in. That was more than $50,000 under the local quote, even after paying for the trip.

He paid his $500. CrowdHealth asked 150 members to fund the remaining $29,500. The money was there in three days, before the procedure.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

They did the shopping. They took the quotes, called other hospitals, and found the $22,000 one. They booked the travel and lined up a local person to drive the couple around once they landed. Then they sent the request to the crowd.

This is the part I love. I've never heard of an insurance company calling three hospitals to find a member a better price. Why would they? It isn't their job.

What's the honest part?

He had to get on a plane for a heart procedure. That's a real ask. Some folks can't travel, or don't want to be far from home for something scary. In a true emergency, you don't get this choice at all. This worked because he was stable enough to plan.

The couple also said they were nervous the whole time. They hadn't seen the crowd come through yet. I think that's normal, and I'd rather tell you than pretend it feels like a sure thing.

Two more notes. This happened in 2022, and CrowdHealth's pricing has changed since then. And the written story and the video description don't match on a couple of small details, like whether 150 or 152 members chipped in. I used the written version.

CrowdHealth says being asked to travel for a big procedure is rare. Its founder put it at around 10 times in 60,000 bills, mostly for folks in very small towns.

The takeaway

Same procedure, $83,655 or $22,000, depending on the building. Prices for the same care can be four times apart, and most of us never find out because nobody shows us the menu. Having someone make those calls is worth a lot.

Will CrowdHealth make me travel for surgery?

Usually not. CrowdHealth says travel requests are rare, roughly 10 in 60,000 bills. But funding is based on a fair price for your area, so if local quotes come in far above that, you may be asked to look farther away or cover the gap. That trade-off is real, and I cover it in what if the crowd doesn't fund your bill.

Why do hospital prices vary so much?

Because prices aren't posted and most patients never ask. Each hospital sets its own sticker price, and the people paying usually aren't the people choosing. I dug into this in why cash prices beat insured prices.

How fast does the crowd fund a bill?

In this story, three days. Across everything, CrowdHealth's August 2026 results showed an average of 7.72 days from a complete bill to money in the member's account. Big, messy hospital bills can take a lot longer to negotiate first.

item.title: The $35,000 Appendix That Cost $500
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member's emergency appendectomy was quoted at $35,000, reduced to $10,600, and cost him $500. What that says about hospital sticker prices.
item.content:encoded:
In short: One member's emergency appendectomy was first quoted at $35,000. CrowdHealth got it reduced to $10,600, he paid his $500, and other members shared the rest. Another member, a doctor, was billed about $50,000 for nine hours in the ER and operating room. Appendix bills are a great lesson in how far apart the sticker price and the real price can be.

Your appendix doesn't schedule anything. It just goes. That makes it a good test of any health plan, because you can't shop around while you're doubled over.

What happened?

CrowdHealth published the story of a married couple who had waited six or seven months before deciding to join. They'd been paying about $450 a month for insurance they rarely used.

Then the husband needed an emergency appendectomy. That's the surgery to take out an appendix before it bursts.

What did the bill look like?

Here are the numbers from their story:

  • First quote: $35,000
  • After it was reduced: $10,600
  • What he paid: $500
  • The rest: shared by other members

That first number isn't a lie exactly. It's a starting bid. Think of a rug at a street market with a $900 tag on it. The seller knows nobody pays $900. The tag is there for whoever doesn't ask.

Is that kind of bill normal?

A second member's public review backs it up. This one was a physician. They described nine hours total, from the ER to the operating room to home, and a bill of about $50,000. They said CrowdHealth had them covered. They didn't say what they paid or what the bill came down to, so I won't guess.

And CrowdHealth's own list of big funded bills includes one for appendicitis that reached $333,943. The list doesn't say what made that one so large.

So the same body part can run $10,600 or $333,000 depending on how it goes and who's asking. That range is the whole reason I want somebody on my side.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

In the first story, they got the price cut from $35,000 to $10,600 using self-pay pricing. Self-pay just means you're paying directly instead of through an insurance company. Hospitals will often take far less from a direct payer, because they get paid faster and skip the paperwork fight.

Then the crowd covered everything above the member's $500.

The couple also said the advocates later pointed them to a doctor who only takes self-pay patients, and they liked him a lot.

What's the honest part?

You don't get the discount at the front desk. In an emergency you get the care, and the negotiating happens afterward, with the bill in your name. That takes some nerve the first time. I'd be lying if I said opening a $35,000 envelope feels fine just because you know the plan.

The second story left out the ending. A doctor saying "they had me covered" is encouraging. It isn't a receipt.

And this first story was chosen and published by CrowdHealth. They pick the good ones. Keep that in mind, the same way you would with any company's testimonials.

The takeaway

A $35,000 quote became $10,600, and the member paid $500. The lesson isn't that surgery is cheap. It's that the first price is rarely the real one, and it helps to have someone whose job is to ask.

How much does an appendectomy cost without insurance?

It varies wildly. In the member stories I found, one was quoted $35,000 and reduced to $10,600, another was billed about $50,000, and the largest on CrowdHealth's published list reached $333,943. The first quote is a starting point, which is why I always ask for the cash price.

What do I pay if I have an emergency surgery on CrowdHealth?

On the standard membership, you pay the first $500 of an eligible health event. The surgery, the ER visit, the scans, and the follow-ups for that same problem all count as one event. Anything above $500 goes to the crowd after the bill is negotiated.

Who negotiates the hospital bill?

CrowdHealth's team does for larger bills, and your care advocate walks you through it. I wrote about that job in what a care advocate actually does. You can also do it yourself with my hospital bill script.

item.title: A Toddler, a Medevac, and $30,000 in Bills
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A dad's toddler was medevacked to a pediatric ICU. Over $30,000 in bills, cut by more than half, and he paid his $500 CrowdHealth commitment.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A dad's 18-month-old son couldn't breathe and was medevacked to a pediatric ICU 90 minutes away. The bills came to more than $30,000. CrowdHealth helped negotiate them down by more than half, the crowd shared what was left, and the dad paid his $500. A couple of bills were still open when he wrote about it.

This is the story that made me want to write this whole series. It's every parent's bad night.

What happened?

A dad wrote a public review earlier this year about his 18-month-old son. The boy had a rough cough and started struggling to breathe. They rushed to the ER in the middle of the night. After about 12 hours on oxygen, the doctors said he needed a pediatric ICU, and it was an hour and a half away. So he went by medevac.

The dad says he asked along the way what all this would cost. He was told not to worry about it. Any parent would have said yes to that ride anyway.

His son got better. Then the mail started coming.

What did the bills look like?

More than $30,000 worth, in several envelopes. That's how hospital billing works. The ER sends one. The medevac company sends one. The ICU sends one. The doctors send their own. It's like a restaurant where the cook, the waiter, and the dishwasher each mail you a separate check.

Here's how the dad says it shook out:

  • Billed: over $30,000
  • After negotiating: cut by more than 50%
  • What he paid: his $500 member commitment
  • The rest: shared by other members

He also said some of the big bills were paid back to him before his own payment to the hospital was even due.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

Two things. First, they negotiated. A hospital's first bill is a sticker price, like the number on a new car window. Almost nobody pays it. Insurance companies don't. Cash payers shouldn't either. I wrote about that in the cash price secret.

Second, once the price was fair, they sent the bills out to the crowd. Other members each chipped in a small amount, and the money landed in his account.

He also mentioned something that shows up in a lot of member reviews. When he had a "what if" question, a real person answered the same day or the next. No hold music.

What's the honest part?

A few things, and the dad said most of them himself.

It wasn't finished. A couple of bills were still being worked on two months later. Big events take a while to close out.

You are the one holding the bills while that happens. Your name is on them, not CrowdHealth's.

And his situation fit the rules. A sudden illness in a healthy kid is exactly what this is built for. He listed the limits in his own review: conditions you already had aren't shared for the first two years, you have to join before a pregnancy, and people 65 and up or who use tobacco can't join.

Why this one sticks with me

His old insurance plan cost about $500 a month just for him, with a $4,000 deductible. He figured a family plan would have run about $1,500 a month with a $12,000 deductible. A deductible is the amount you pay yourself before insurance pays a dime. So on that plan, this same night could have cost him $12,000 on top of the monthly bill.

Instead it was $500. That's the whole pitch, in one bad night.

The takeaway

When a kid can't breathe, nobody shops for prices. The shopping happens after, and this dad had someone doing it for him. More than $30,000 billed, cut by more than half, $500 out of pocket. Not finished yet when he wrote it, and not guaranteed. But it worked the way he was told it would.

Questions I get about this

Does CrowdHealth cover ambulance or helicopter rides?

In this member's story, the medevac was part of the health event and its bill was handled with the others. One limit I do know: CrowdHealth's member guide says international air ambulance is not eligible. Read the current guide, because it's the rulebook.

Do I have to pay the hospital first and wait?

Often you pay and get paid back. For bigger bills, CrowdHealth says it can negotiate before you pay anything. This dad said some large bills were funded before his payment was due. I walk through the steps in how one health event gets paid.

What should I do in a real emergency?

Go. Get care first and sort out the money later. No plan of any kind is worth a delay when someone can't breathe. I wrote a step-by-step for this in health sharing and the ER.

item.title: Is CrowdHealth Legit? What I Found When I Checked
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: CrowdHealth has funded 53,877 bills at a 99.8% rate with 4.9 stars on Trustpilot. It's real. It's also not insurance, with no legal guarantee. The honest check.
item.content:encoded:
In short: Yes, in the sense that matters: it's a real company doing exactly what it says. 53,877 bills funded, 99.8 percent of submissions funded, 4.9 stars on Trustpilot, about 35,000 members. But "legit" and "insurance" are different questions. Nobody is legally required to fund your bill, and no state regulator can help you if they don't. That's the actual trade.

"Is this a scam?" is the first thing anybody asks me about CrowdHealth, and it's the right question to ask about anything that promises to replace a $1,500 premium.

So let's check it properly. I'm a member, my family of four has used it since 2022, and I earn a referral if you join through me. Weigh that, and then look at the evidence yourself.

The short answer

CrowdHealth is a real, operating company that does what it describes. It isn't a scam.

It's also not insurance, doesn't claim to be, and doesn't carry the protections insurance carries. Both of those things are true at once, and the second one is the part that should actually drive your decision.

The track record

Numbers first, because they're checkable.

  • 53,877 bills funded. That's a lot of real money moving to real people.
  • 99.8 percent of submitted bills get funded.
  • About 35,000 members.
  • 4.9 stars on Trustpilot.
  • About $100 million saved versus traditional insurance, which is CrowdHealth's own figure and should be read as a company claim, not an audit.

Sit with the first and third for a second. Fifty-three thousand bills across about thirty-five thousand members is about three funded bills for every two members. That's not a program where a handful of people use it and everybody else just pays in. The crowd is actually working.

I'll admit something here. I've had the member count wrong on this site before, once too high and once too low, because I picked up a number and didn't recheck it. The 35,000 figure is what CrowdHealth's CEO said in a September 2026 webinar, along with about 40,000 people who have ever joined.

What "legit" doesn't mean

Here's where most reviews stop, and where I think they do you a disservice.

A strong track record is evidence about the past. It's not a contract about your future. The distinction matters more than anything else on this page, so let me put it plainly.

When you buy insurance, you're buying two things: the money, and the referee.

The referee is a state agency with the power to make a company pay you. You never think about it until you need it, and most people never need it. But it exists.

CrowdHealth has the money part, and the record above says the money part works. It does not have the referee. There's no legal obligation for anybody to fund your bill, and there's no government office to call if they don't.

That's not a loophole somebody discovered. It's stated plainly in the actual terms, and it's the trade you're making. The cost is lower partly because that machinery isn't there.

Maryland's insurance regulator published a consumer advisory about CrowdHealth (opens in a new tab) in March 2026 making essentially this point. I'd rather you read it yourself than take my summary or the company's.

It isn't a health sharing ministry either

Worth knowing, because it changes how you read other reviews.

Most comparison sites file CrowdHealth under "health sharing plans" next to the faith-based programs. CrowdHealth's own term for itself is healthcare crowdfunding, and it's not a ministry: it's for-profit, and there's no shared-beliefs requirement.

That's not trivia. Many states carve out a legal exception specifically for sharing ministries on religious grounds. CrowdHealth doesn't get that carve-out, which is exactly what Maryland's notice turns on. If a review treats it as a ministry, that review hasn't understood the product.

How to check it yourself

Don't take my word for any of this. It takes twenty minutes:

  1. Read the member guide, especially the sections on eligibility and conditions you already have. The limits are stated, not buried.
  2. Read Trustpilot, and read the one-star reviews, not just the average. Look for whether complaints are about the rules being unfair or about the rules being hidden. Those are very different problems.

item.title: CrowdHealth and Pre-Existing Conditions: The Real Rules
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: CrowdHealth funds nothing for pre-existing conditions in years 1-2, then $25,000/yr from year 3. The 5-year window, and the cholesterol and blood pressure exemption.
item.content:encoded:
In short: Anything documented, diagnosed, symptomatic, suspected, or treated within five years of joining CrowdHealth gets no funding in years one and two, then up to $25,000 a year from year three on. High cholesterol and high blood pressure are explicitly exempt. If you have a real ongoing condition, this rule is usually the whole answer, and the answer is often no.

This is the rule that decides it for most people, and it's the one most reviews gloss over. So I'm going to give you CrowdHealth's actual language, not my summary of it, and then tell you what I think it means for you.

I'm a member. My family of four has used CrowdHealth since 2022. I'd rather you read this and walk away than join and find out in an emergency room.

What the rule actually says

CrowdHealth's term is Previously Documented, Diagnosed, or Symptomatic conditions. Their guidelines say the crowd welcomes members with varied health backgrounds, but there are limits on funding health events tied to these conditions.

Here's the shape of it:

  • The window is five years before you join.
  • It covers anything diagnosed, documented, symptomatic, suspected, or treated in that window. Note "suspected." You don't need a formal diagnosis for this to apply.
  • Years one and two of membership: not eligible for funding. Not reduced. Not eligible.
  • Year three and after: a $25,000 per year crowdfunding cap for anything related to those conditions.

Their own examples, and they're clear the list isn't exhaustive: asthma, congenital conditions, diabetes, genetic disorders, heart conditions, sleep apnea.

One of those is about to get its own rule. Starting January 1, 2027, Type 2 diabetes care won't be eligible for crowdfunding on the standard membership at all, even for a new diagnosis. Members who want help with it move to a separate CrowdHealth program called Exit Diabetes.

Children who join CrowdHealth at birth are excepted from the congenital condition limit.

The exemption almost nobody mentions

High cholesterol and high blood pressure are not subject to these limits.

I want to put that on its own line, because those two are the single most common thing a 45-year-old is quietly worried about when they read a pre-existing clause. If your doctor has you on a statin or a blood pressure pill and you assumed that disqualified you, it doesn't.

I've read a lot of CrowdHealth write-ups. Almost none of them mention this. It's in the guidelines.

What "suspected" means for you, practically

This is the part I'd think hardest about.

The rule doesn't require a diagnosis. If something was symptomatic, or a doctor suspected it and wrote it down, it's inside the window. That means the honest question isn't "what am I diagnosed with." It's "what is in my chart from the last five years."

Most people don't actually know. So before you cancel anything:

  1. Request your records from your primary care doctor for the last five years.
  2. Read what's written there, including notes about things that turned out to be nothing.
  3. Ask CrowdHealth directly, in writing, about anything you find. Get the answer in writing too.

That third step is the important one. Do not rely on a blog post, mine included, for a question this specific to your body.

What this rule is actually for

It's easy to read this as the company weaseling. I don't think that's what it is, and it's worth understanding the logic, because it tells you what the product is.

CrowdHealth isn't insurance, and it isn't legally required to take all comers the way an ACA plan is. Its costs stay low because the crowd is mostly funding unexpected things. If somebody could join the month after a serious diagnosis and have the crowd pick up an ongoing treatment, the monthly ask for everybody else would climb until the thing stopped working.

That's the trade. It's cheap partly because it doesn't do this. Knowing that doesn't help you if you're the one with the condition, but it does tell you the rule isn't going to get quietly relaxed.

Who this rule disqualifies

Be honest with yourself here:

  • Anyone with a chronic condition needing ongoing treatment. Two years of nothing, then a $25,000 annual ceiling, is not coverage for diabetes or a heart condition. It's a partial subsidy starting two years from now.
  • Anyone in the middle of a workup. If you're currently being investigated for something, it's symptomatic or suspected now, which puts it in the window.
  • Anyone who'd be gambling. If you're hoping the rule won't be applied to you, don't join. It'll be applied.

If that's you, the honest answer is a real insurance plan, and I'd rather say so than take the referral. There's more in who health sharing is wrong for.

Who it doesn't disqualify

  • Reasonably healthy people whose charts are boring.
  • People managing only cholesterol or blood pressure, per the exemption above.
  • People whose past issue is more than five years back and has stayed quiet.
  • Anything genuinely new that happens after you join. That's the main event, and it's funded normally.

The part I have to say

Even outside these rules, CrowdHealth is not insurance. There's no legal guarantee any bill gets funded, and no state regulator to call if one doesn't. The record is strong, 53,877 bills funded at a 99.8 percent rate, but a record is not a promise.

The whole picture, including costs and the monthly cap, is on my CrowdHealth guide.

Does CrowdHealth cover pre-existing conditions?

Not in years one and two. From year three, up to $25,000 a year for conditions documented, diagnosed, symptomatic, suspected, or treated within five years of joining.

How far back does CrowdHealth look?

Five years before your join date.

Does high blood pressure disqualify me from CrowdHealth?

No. High blood pressure and high cholesterol are explicitly exempt from the previously documented, diagnosed, or symptomatic limits.

What if I was never formally diagnosed?

The rule covers conditions that were symptomatic or suspected, not just diagnosed. Pull your medical records and ask CrowdHealth in writing before you join.

Is asthma a pre-existing condition for CrowdHealth?

Asthma is on their own list of examples, so yes, if it was documented, diagnosed, or symptomatic within five years of joining.

What about a baby born after I join?

Children who become members at birth are excepted from the congenital condition limitation.

item.title: How Much Does CrowdHealth Cost? The Real Numbers, With the Cap
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: CrowdHealth costs $60/mo per person plus a capped crowd contribution. Worst case is $200/mo under 55, $340 at 55-64, $660 for a family of four. Real math.
item.content:encoded:
In short: CrowdHealth costs $60 a month per person, children included, plus a crowd contribution that's hard-capped by age and household. Under 55 your worst possible month is $200. From 55 to 64 it's $340. For a family of four or more it's $660. On top of that you cover the first $500 of any health event. The crowd usually asks for less than the cap.

Every time somebody asks me what CrowdHealth costs, I give them a number, and then I watch them not believe it. So let me do this the long way, with the arithmetic in the open.

My family of four has been on it since 2022. Here's exactly how the money works.

The three pieces

One. The subscription: $60 a month, per person.

Children count. A family of four pays $240 a month in subscription. This is the part that doesn't move. It pays for the app, the people who negotiate your bills down, and a Care Advocate you can actually reach.

It does not go up because you got older, and it does not go up because you got sick.

Two. The crowd contribution: variable, but capped.

Each month you chip in to fund other members' bills. That's the crowdfunding part, and it's the number people worry about, because "variable" sounds like "unlimited."

It isn't. There's a published ceiling.

Three. The member commitment: $500 per health event.

A health event is one thing that happens to you. A broken wrist. An appendix. You cover the first $500 of it, and the crowd covers the eligible rest. It works like a deductible, except it resets per event instead of per year, and it's $500 instead of five figures.

The cap, which is the part nobody tells you

Who you areMost the crowd can ask in one monthYour worst case, with the $60
Ages 0 to 54$140$200 per person
Ages 55 to 64$280$340 per person
A family of four or more$420 for the whole household$660 for the family

Read the bottom row twice. A family of four pays $240 in subscription, and the crowd can ask for at most $420 more. Six hundred sixty dollars is the worst month that family can possibly have. Then $500 on top if somebody actually gets hurt that month.

That's the ceiling. It is not the normal month. CrowdHealth has historically not asked for the full amount, and in a quiet month the ask is a good bit lower.

For a real month: in October 2026, CrowdHealth told members the all-in cost was $165 for a single member under 55, $270 for a single member 55 or older, and $555 for a family of four, before a small transaction fee.

One change is already announced. On January 1, 2027, the subscription goes from $60 to $65 per person. If the crowd caps stay where they are, the worst cases become $205, $345, and $680. I'll update this page when the 2027 caps are published.

Let's do it for real people

A 35-year-old on her own. $60 subscription. Worst month, $200. If she breaks an ankle in March, add $500 that one time. Her worst possible year, assuming the crowd maxed her out every single month and she got hurt once, is $2,400 plus $500, so $2,900.

Now price a bronze marketplace plan for a 35-year-old without a subsidy. The premium alone often beats $2,900 before the deductible does one thing for her.

A 58-year-old bridging to Medicare. $60 subscription, but his cap is $280, so his worst month is $340 and his worst year is $4,080 plus commitments. That's a real step up from the under-55 number, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't. Then go price an individual plan for a 58-year-old. It's frequently north of a thousand dollars a month. The gap is still enormous. More on that in health sharing for early retirees.

A family of four, two adults under 55. $240 subscription. Worst month $660. Worst year $7,920, before any $500 commitments.

Compare that to a family plan with a $1,500 monthly premium and a $12,000 deductible, which is $18,000 before the plan pays for anything. That comparison is why we switched.

Where the savings actually come from

It isn't magic, and it isn't the crowd being generous. Two things do the work.

Cash prices. When you walk in as self-pay instead of insured, the price is often dramatically lower for the identical service. Discounts commonly run 25 to 85 percent off billed charges. CrowdHealth's team negotiates this for you before the crowd ever sees the bill, which means the crowd is funding a smaller number. I wrote about the mechanism in why cash prices beat insured prices.

Aligned incentives. CrowdHealth makes its money on that flat $60, not on a slice of your claims. Nobody there gets a bonus for slow-walking your bill. That's the whole argument in nobody gets paid to make you well.

What the price does not buy you

I'd be selling you something if I stopped here.

The low number is low partly because you're giving something up, and it's a real thing. There is no legal guarantee your bill gets funded. CrowdHealth is not insurance. No state insurance regulator can step in for you if a bill goes unfunded.

The funding rate is 99.8 percent across 53,877 bills, which is a strong record. A record is not a promise, and I won't dress it up as one.

You're also not buying coverage for a condition you already have. Anything documented, diagnosed, or symptomatic within five years of joining gets nothing in years one and two, then up to $25,000 a year from year three. High cholesterol and high blood pressure are exempt. If that rule lands on you, the cheap monthly number is beside the point.

The full picture, including who should walk away, is on my CrowdHealth guide.

So is it cheaper?

For a reasonably healthy household with a cushion, on our numbers, by a lot.

For somebody with an ongoing condition, or somebody getting a large ACA subsidy, quite possibly not. Run your own numbers before you cancel anything, and read who health sharing is wrong for first.

Questions I get about this

How much is CrowdHealth per month?

$60 per person in subscription, children included, plus a capped crowd contribution. Worst case all in is $200 a month under 55, $340 from 55 to 64, and $660 for a family of four or more. Most months come in under the cap.

Does CrowdHealth cost more as you get older?

The $60 subscription is the same at any age. The cap is not. It's $140 up to 54 and $280 from 55 to 64, so crossing 55 moves your worst month from $200 to $340.

Is there a deductible?

No. There's a $500 member commitment per health event instead, and it resets per event rather than per year.

How much does CrowdHealth cost for a family?

$60 per person, so $240 for a family of four, plus a household crowd cap of $420. That's $660 in the worst month.

Yes, and it's published by age and household size. That cap is the direct answer to the usual objection that crowdfunding has no out-of-pocket maximum. On the monthly side, it does.

All month we've dug into health sharing from every angle: the costs, the limits, the ER, the pre-existing rules, the numbers, the peace of mind. Let's bring it home. Here's a simple five-question guide that pulls it all together. Answer these honestly, and you'll know whether health sharing is right for your family, no guru required. This is the whole month, boiled down.

Question 1: Are you and your family generally healthy?

This is the big one. Health sharing rewards the relatively healthy and is a poor fit for someone who needs constant, costly care right now. If you're mostly healthy with the normal bumps of life, that's a strong yes. If someone has a serious active condition, lean no, or keep guaranteed coverage for that person. Question 2: Can you keep $500 on hand at all times?

Health sharing asks you to cover the first $500 of any health event. If you can keep that liquid, ideally with a small emergency fund on top, you're built for this model. If money is so tight that $500 would be a crisis, shore that up first before switching. This is the foundation everything else stands on.

Question 3: Are you okay trading a legal guarantee for a big cost savings?

This is the honest heart of it. Health sharing is not insurance. There's no legal guarantee your bill gets funded, though the track record is strong, with tens of thousands of bills paid. If a strong-but-not-guaranteed backstop at a fraction of the cost sounds like a smart trade, yes. If the lack of a guarantee would haunt you, that's real information, and no is a fine answer.

Question 4: Are your prescriptions and needs a fit?

Quick gut check on the recurring stuff. Are your regular medications cheap generics, and is your routine care the normal kind? Then yes. Do you rely on an expensive ongoing brand-name drug or heavy specialized care every month? Then the model, which is built for events, may not fit that piece. Question 5: Are you willing to be a little hands-on?

Health sharing works best for people willing to ask for the cash price, read the guidelines, and keep a cushion. It's not "set it and forget it." If you're okay being a bit more involved in your own care and bills, yes. If you truly want to hand it all off and never think about it, weigh that honestly.

Mostly yeses? Health sharing is very likely a strong, money-saving fit for your family, and worth a real look. A few hard nos, especially on questions 1 or 3? Then it's probably not your tool right now, and that's completely fine. The goal was never to talk you into anything. It was to hand you the plain-English version so you could decide for yourself. The takeaway

Five questions: Are you healthy? Can you keep $500 ready? Are you okay trading a guarantee for big savings? Do your meds and needs fit? Are you willing to be a little hands-on? The rule for a fair comparison

People compare healthcare wrong all the time. They look at the monthly bill and stop there. But the monthly bill is only half the story. To compare honestly, you have to add up everything you'd actually pay across a whole year, in both the good scenario and the bad one.

So we'll do two versions of the year: a healthy year where little happens, and a rougher year with one real health event. That's the only fair way to see it.

item.title: Letting Go of the "What If"
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: No coverage erases risk. How to let go of the healthcare "what if": trade vague fear for a concrete plan, control what you can, and release what you can't.
item.content:encoded:
In short: No coverage on earth erases risk. Insurance doesn't, health sharing doesn't, being rich doesn't. The goal isn't zero worry. It's turning the vague "what if" into a concrete plan: pay my $500, let the advocate negotiate, get care first in an emergency, cover gaps with the emergency fund, pay cash for routine. Do the controllable part well, then set the rest down.

I want to talk about the quiet thing underneath all these health and money decisions. It's not really about premiums or deductibles or crowd funding. It's about the "what if" that runs in the back of your mind. What if something big happens? What if I picked wrong? That worry is heavy, and I've carried it too. So let me talk honestly about how to set it down, whatever coverage you end up choosing.

The "what if" never fully goes away, and that's okay

Here's the first honest thing. No coverage on earth erases risk. Insurance doesn't. Health sharing doesn't. Being rich doesn't. Life comes with uncertainty, and any product promising to make you totally safe is lying to you.

So the goal was never zero worry. The goal is to worry about the right size of thing, and to know you've done the reasonable stuff a responsible person can do. Once you've done that, the leftover worry is just the tax we all pay for being alive, and you're allowed to put it down.

Trade the vague fear for a concrete plan

Vague worry is the worst kind, because your brain fills the blank with the scariest possible movie. The fix is to make the fear concrete, because a concrete problem has a concrete answer.

So instead of "what if something awful happens," write down the actual plan:

  • If a health event hits, I pay my $500, and my advocate negotiates the bill down.
  • If it's an emergency, I get care first and sort the paperwork after.
  • If there's a gap, my emergency fund covers it.
  • If it's routine, I pay the cash price.

Suddenly the monster under the bed is just a list. Lists aren't scary. I built my own version of that list as a layered safety net.

Control what you can, release what you can't

There's real freedom in sorting your worries into two buckets.

In the "I can control this" bucket: keeping $500 liquid, reading the guidelines, asking for the cash price, choosing coverage that fits your health honestly. Do these, fully, and take the win.

In the "I can't control this" bucket: whether you get sick, when, and the exact shape of the future. You cannot think your way to certainty about these, so spending your peace on them is just paying twice. Do the first bucket well, and you earn the right to release the second.

Why this matters for your actual health

This isn't just feel-good talk. Chronic worry about money and health is its own kind of tax on your body and your sleep. Part of why my family landed where we did is that a simple, understandable plan let us stop white-knuckling it. Knowing the shape of the deal, limits and all, is what let me actually relax. That peace is a real benefit, not a soft one.

The takeaway

You will never buy your way to zero risk, so stop trying. Instead, do the reasonable things a responsible person can do, turn the vague "what if" into a concrete plan, and then genuinely let the rest go. You've done your part. Carrying the worry on top of the plan doesn't make you safer. It just makes you tired. Set it down.

Questions I get about this

How do I stop worrying about medical bills?

Make the fear concrete. Vague worry lets your brain fill the blank with the scariest movie. Write down the actual plan for each scenario, and the monster under the bed becomes a list. Lists aren't scary. I built mine as a layered safety net.

Is health sharing riskier than insurance?

item.title: Budgeting When You're Self-Insured
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: On a high deductible or health sharing, you're self-insured. The habit that makes it work is a healthcare sinking fund: park your event number, build a buffer.
item.content:encoded:
In short: If you're on a high-deductible plan or health sharing, you're partly self-insured, and the habit that makes it work is a healthcare sinking fund. Park your event number ($500 on health sharing), build a buffer of a few thousand on top, automate a small monthly transfer to a separate account, and feed it with the premiums you're no longer paying.

"Self-insured" sounds fancy, but it just means this: you've decided to cover some of your own risk instead of paying a company to cover all of it. Anyone with a high deductible is partly self-insured already. Anyone on health sharing is too. The trick that makes it work isn't luck. It's a boring little budgeting habit that turns scary surprise bills into planned-for expenses. Here's how to do it.

The one idea that makes self-insuring work

It's called a sinking fund. Fancy name, simple idea: you save a little money every month toward an expense you know is coming eventually, even if you don't know exactly when.

You already do this without thinking. You know your car will need tires and brakes someday, so a smart person sets aside a bit each month instead of panicking when it happens. Your health works the same way. You don't know when a health event will hit, but you know one eventually will. So you fund for it on purpose, ahead of time.

How to build your healthcare sinking fund

Here's the simple version I'd follow:

  • Start with your event number. If you're on health sharing, that's your $500 per-event commitment. Get that amount parked and keep it there, always ready.
  • Add a buffer on top. Aim to build past the single event toward a cushion of a few thousand, so two things in one year, or a gap, never wrecks you.
  • Automate a small monthly transfer. Even a modest amount each month into a separate savings account adds up fast and quietly. This ties right into the DIY safety net I laid out.
  • Keep it separate and boring. A different account you don't touch. Out of sight, so you're not tempted to raid it for a vacation.

Where the money comes from

Here's the quiet win. When you self-insure well, your regular monthly healthcare cost usually drops, because you're not paying fat premiums. That gap between what you used to pay and what you pay now is exactly what feeds the sinking fund. You're not finding new money. You're redirecting the savings into your own cushion instead of a company's pocket.

Do that, and over a year or two you build a personal buffer that does the job people think only insurance can do for the small and medium stuff.

The honest caution

Self-insuring works great for the small and medium bumps. It does not, by itself, cover a true catastrophe. That's why the sinking fund is a layer, not the whole plan. You still want real coverage for the big stuff behind it, whether that's insurance or health sharing. The budget habit protects the front line. It's not the whole army.

The takeaway

Budgeting when you're self-insured comes down to one habit: a healthcare sinking fund. Park your event number, build a buffer on top, automate a small monthly transfer, and feed it with the money you save on premiums. It turns "surprise" bills into ones you already planned for. Boring, quiet, and exactly the kind of thing that lets normal families sleep at night.

What is a sinking fund?

Saving a little every month toward an expense you know is coming eventually, even if you don't know exactly when. You already do it for tires and brakes. Your health works the same way: you don't know when a health event will hit, but you know one eventually will.

How much should be in my healthcare sinking fund?

Start with your event number and keep it parked. Then build past it toward a cushion of a few thousand, so two events in one year, or a gap, never wrecks you. It's a layer in the DIY healthcare safety net, not the whole plan.

Where does the money for the sinking fund come from?

From the gap between what you used to pay in premiums and what you pay now. You're not finding new money. You're redirecting savings into your own cushion instead of a company's pocket.

item.title: Health Sharing vs. COBRA
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: COBRA keeps your old plan at the brutal full price. Healthy and bridging a job gap? Health sharing does it for a fraction. Mid-treatment? Keep COBRA.
item.content:encoded:
In short: COBRA keeps your exact work plan after you leave a job, but you pay the full price your employer used to hide, often well over a thousand dollars a month for a family. If you're healthy and just bridging to the next job, health sharing usually does it for a fraction. If you're mid-treatment or need an ironclad guarantee, keep COBRA.

If you've ever lost or left a job, you've met COBRA, and you probably remember the sticker shock. COBRA lets you keep your old work health insurance for a while after you leave, which sounds great until you see the price. Suddenly you're paying the full cost your employer used to hide from you, and it's brutal. When that letter shows up, health sharing is worth a serious look. Let me compare them honestly.

What COBRA actually is

At your job, your employer quietly pays a big chunk of your health insurance. You only ever saw your small slice on the pay stub. COBRA lets you keep that exact same plan after you leave, but now you pay the whole thing yourself, employer's share included, plus a little admin fee on top.

So the coverage doesn't change. The price just triples or worse, because the hidden subsidy is gone. For a family, COBRA can easily run well over a thousand dollars a month, sometimes closer to two.

The case for COBRA

I'll give it its due. COBRA has real advantages in specific situations:

  • It's the same plan and network, so your doctors and any ongoing treatment continue seamlessly.
  • It's real insurance, with a legal guarantee and your accumulated deductible for the year.
  • It's the right call mid-treatment. If you're in the middle of a serious health situation, do not switch away from real coverage to save money. Keep COBRA.

COBRA exists for continuity, and continuity is exactly what you want when something is already going on.

The case for health sharing instead

But if you're healthy and just need a bridge to your next job or plan, COBRA's price is punishing for what you get. Here's where health sharing shines:

  • The cost is a fraction of COBRA. With CrowdHealth, the service I use, it's $60 per person per month plus a modest crowd contribution, not a four-figure premium.
  • It's not tied to a job you no longer have, so it doesn't end when your COBRA window runs out.
  • You get real human help with bills through a care advocate, which I wrote about in what a care advocate actually does.

For a healthy person between jobs, paying COBRA prices can feel like lighting money on fire.

The honest deciding factor

It really comes down to two questions. Are you healthy right now, and can you handle a bit of risk for a big cost savings? If yes, health sharing is often the smarter bridge. Are you mid-treatment or do you need an ironclad guarantee right now? Then COBRA's price buys you something real, and it's worth it. Because health sharing is not insurance, there's no legal guarantee, so this choice really hinges on your current health. Here is my honest fit test.

The takeaway

COBRA keeps your exact plan but charges you the brutal full price, which makes sense only when you need continuity, like being mid-treatment. If you're healthy and just bridging a gap between jobs, health sharing usually does the job for a fraction of the cost, and it isn't tied to the job you left. Match the tool to your situation, and don't overpay for a guarantee you may not need.

Why is COBRA so expensive?

Because the hidden employer subsidy is gone. At your job, your employer quietly paid a big chunk of the premium. COBRA lets you keep the same plan, but now you pay the whole thing yourself, employer's share included, plus a small admin fee.

When is COBRA the right choice?

When you need continuity. It's the same plan and network, it's real insurance with a legal guarantee, and it keeps the deductible you've already paid toward this year. If you're in the middle of a serious health situation, do not switch away from real coverage to save money.

Does health sharing end when my COBRA window would?

No. Health sharing isn't tied to a job you no longer have, so it doesn't expire after the COBRA period. It moves with you to the next job, self-employment, or whatever comes next.

item.title: Dental and Vision Without Insurance
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: The dentist and glasses without insurance: ask for the cash price, try a dental savings plan, buy glasses online, add a cheap standalone plan only if needed.
item.content:encoded:
In short: Dental and vision are the easy part of going without insurance because they're predictable, not emergencies. Ask the dentist for the cash price or use a dental savings plan. Pay for the eye exam directly, then buy glasses online for a fraction of the shop price. Add a cheap standalone dental or vision plan only if your family truly needs a lot of work.

Dental and vision are the two things that trip people up when they think about leaving traditional insurance, or when they go with health sharing, which doesn't cover routine dental and vision. So people panic a little: "How will I afford the dentist and my glasses?" Take a breath. This stuff is way more manageable to pay for directly than the big medical scary stuff. Here's exactly how my family handles it, no insurance required.

The mindset: these are predictable, so budget them

Here's the key insight. Dental cleanings and eye exams aren't surprise emergencies. You know they're coming. A cleaning twice a year, an eye exam once a year, new glasses every couple of years. Predictable costs don't need insurance, they need a plan. And they're small enough that a plan is easy.

Insurance is for the unpredictable and expensive. Routine dental and vision are the opposite of that, which is exactly why paying directly usually works out fine.

Dental: just ask for the cash price

Most routine dental work is affordable at the cash price if you ask. A cleaning, exam, and X-rays as a cash-pay patient is often a very reasonable number, sometimes cheaper than what you were paying in monthly dental insurance premiums for coverage you barely used.

A few ways to keep it cheap:

  • Ask for the cash or self-pay price up front. Same trick that works everywhere in healthcare.
  • Consider a dental savings plan. Not insurance, just a membership that gets you discounted rates at participating dentists for a small annual fee.
  • Check a dental school near you for low-cost cleanings done by supervised students.

Vision: shop like it's any other purchase

Eye care splits into two easy parts. The exam, and the glasses or contacts.

Dental and vision feel scary without insurance, but they're actually the easy part. They're predictable, so you budget for them. Ask for the cash price, shop for glasses like any other purchase, and add a cheap standalone plan only if you truly need one. The dentist and the eye doctor are not the reason to fear leaving traditional insurance.

The fastest way to trust something is to hear its honest limits before you hear its pitch. The big categories that aren't shared

  • Expensive ongoing medications. The model funds events, not a predictable high monthly drug cost forever. More on health sharing and prescriptions.

None of these should feel like a trap. They're all the same theme: health sharing is built for the unexpected big stuff, not for routine, predictable, or elective costs.

A sharing community pools money to catch each other when something unexpected and expensive hits. If the pool also paid for everyone's glasses, teeth cleanings, and elective procedures, it would just be regular insurance with regular insurance prices, and the whole cost advantage would vanish.

CrowdHealth doesn't cover routine dental and vision, cosmetic work, expensive ongoing meds, or pre-existing conditions before their waiting periods. Know the gaps, plan the cheap workarounds, and you get the best of it: a strong, affordable backstop for the big stuff, with no nasty surprises.

item.title: Why Cash Prices Beat Insured Prices
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: Why the cash price often beats the insured price for the same procedure: it's the real price with the insurance hassle stripped out. How to use it every time.
item.content:encoded:
In short: The same procedure at the same hospital can cost less if you pay cash than if you run it through insurance. The sticker price is built for the insurance fight: claims, denials, resubmissions, overhead. The cash price strips all that out. If a bill is under your deductible, you're paying it yourself anyway, so ask for the cash price and compare.

Here's a thing that sounds impossible until you see it happen. The same procedure, at the same hospital, can cost more when you run it through insurance than when you just pay cash. I'm not exaggerating and I'm not talking about a rare edge case. It happens all the time, and once you understand why, you'll never look at a medical bill the same way again.

Two prices for the same thing

Every hospital basically keeps two prices. There's the sticker price, a big scary number aimed at insurance companies. And there's the cash price, the number they'll take from someone paying directly, today, without the insurance paperwork.

The cash price is often a fraction of the sticker. Not ten percent off. Sometimes half, sometimes a lot less than half. Same MRI, same room, same doctor.

Why the gap exists

It comes down to who's paying and how much hassle is involved.

When insurance is in the mix, there's a whole expensive dance. The hospital bills high, the insurer negotiates down, claims get processed, some get denied and resubmitted, and everyone budgets for the fight. That overhead gets baked into the sticker price.

When you pay cash, all of that disappears. No claims, no waiting, no chasing. The hospital gets paid now, for certain, with no paperwork. That certainty is worth a discount to them, so they give you one. You're not begging for charity. You're offering them the thing they like best, which is money now with zero hassle.

The counterintuitive part

This is why "I have insurance" is not always the cheapest way to pay. If a bill is smaller than your deductible, you're paying the whole thing out of pocket anyway, and you might be paying the inflated insured rate while you do it. In that spot, asking for the cash price can literally save you money over using your own insurance. Weird, but true.

How to actually use this

You don't need to be an expert. You just need to ask one question before any non-emergency care: "What's the cash or self-pay price?" Then compare it to what you'd owe through insurance. Sometimes insurance wins, sometimes cash wins. The point is you check instead of assuming. And if you get a big bill, this is the foundation for negotiating it down step by step.

The takeaway

The cash price isn't a secret discount for the poor. It's the real price with the hassle stripped out, and anyone can ask for it. The sticker price is built for the insurance fight. When you're paying out of pocket, you're not in that fight, so don't pay the price that was built for it. Ask for cash, every time.

Questions I get about this

Why does a hospital charge less for cash?

Because money now with zero hassle is worth a discount to them. No claims, no waiting, no chasing. When insurance is in the mix there's a whole expensive dance, and that overhead gets baked into the sticker price. You're not begging for charity. You're offering the thing they like best.

Should I use my insurance or pay cash?

Check both. Before any non-emergency care, ask "What's the cash or self-pay price?" and compare it to what you'd owe through insurance. If the bill is smaller than your deductible, cash often wins. If you're close to your out-of-pocket max, insurance may win. The point is you check instead of assuming.

How much cheaper is the cash price?

Often a fraction of the sticker. Not ten percent off. Sometimes half, sometimes a lot less than half. Same MRI, same room, same doctor. Care advocates negotiating on behalf of health sharing members commonly see 25 to 85 percent off list price.

item.title: Pre-Existing Conditions and Health Sharing: The Real Rules

In short: Pre-existing conditions are health sharing's most important limit. A condition you already have, or had recently, isn't shared right away. There's a waiting period, and if you go a stretch without symptoms, treatment, or medication, it can gradually become eligible over the first few years. This is the topic where you most need a straight shooter, because it's where health sharing has its biggest, most important limit. So no spin here, just how it actually works with CrowdHealth, the service I use, and how to think about whether it's right for you.

First, what counts as pre-existing

A pre-existing condition is any health issue you already have when you sign up, or one you had recently. Think diabetes, high blood pressure, a past cancer, a bad back you've been treated for. The reason it matters is simple. Health sharing is a community pooling money for unexpected events. Something you already have isn't unexpected, so the model treats it differently.

That's not a moral judgment about you. It's just the math of how a sharing pool stays fair for everyone in it.

The waiting-period rule

Here's the core mechanic. Many conditions aren't eligible for sharing right away. Instead there's a waiting period, and if you go a stretch of time without symptoms, treatment, or medication for that condition, it can gradually become eligible over the first few years of membership.

In plain terms: the longer you're a healthy member without needing care for that condition, the more it may be shared later. A well-managed issue from years ago is treated very differently from something you're actively being treated for today.

Read the actual guidelines, not a summary

I can give you the shape of it, but your specific condition deserves the specific rule. The guidelines spell out exactly how each type of situation is handled and how long the waiting periods run. Read them before you join. This is the single most important homework assignment in the whole decision, and skipping it is how people get an unwelcome surprise later. That's also why I keep pointing people to my honest who-should-skip-this post.

When health sharing is the wrong tool

Let me be blunt, because you deserve it. If you have a serious, active condition that needs ongoing, expensive care right now, health sharing is probably not your best fit for that condition today. You'd likely be better served by a plan with a legal guarantee. There's no shame in that. Using the right tool for your situation is the smart move, and sometimes health sharing isn't it.

When it can still work

On the other hand, if your "pre-existing condition" is something minor, well-controlled, or years behind you, it may matter far less than you fear, especially after the waiting period. Plenty of people with a manageable history use health sharing happily for everything else life throws at them. The only way to know your case is to read the rule for your specific condition.

The self-employed math problem

When you have a normal job, your employer quietly pays a big chunk of your health insurance. You only see your slice. The day you go out on your own, that hidden subsidy disappears and you're staring at the whole bill. For a family, an individual market plan can run well over a thousand dollars a month, with a deductible waiting behind it.

For a healthy self-employed person or family, health sharing solves the exact pain the 1099 life creates: a high, unpredictable healthcare cost that isn't tied to any employer. A flat monthly number, real human help with bills, and coverage that's truly yours. Mind the tax difference, know the limits, and it can be one of the smartest moves you make working for yourself.

item.title: The DIY Healthcare Safety Net
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: You don't need one perfect plan. Build three layers: an emergency fund, the habit of asking for the cash price, and real coverage for the big stuff.
item.content:encoded:
In short: You don't need one magic product to protect your family from a health disaster. You need three layers: an emergency fund you can reach fast, the habit of asking for the cash price, and a real plan for the big stuff, whether that's insurance or health sharing. When you have layers, one weak spot doesn't sink you.

Here's a mindset that changed how I think about all of this. You don't need one magic product to protect your family from a health disaster. You need a few simple layers that work together. Firefighters don't rely on one thing, they've got the alarm, the extinguisher, and the exit plan. Your healthcare safety net can work the same way, and you can start building it today no matter what plan you're on.

Layer one: a real emergency fund

This is the floor everything else stands on. Cash you can reach fast, set aside only for "oh no" moments. Even a first $1,000 changes everything, because it turns a crisis into an inconvenience.

If you use health sharing, this is where your $500 event commitment lives, ready to go. If you're on insurance, this is what covers the deductible you'd owe before the plan helps. Either way, you want this cushion. Start small and keep feeding it.

Layer two: knowing the cash price

The single most expensive mistake in American healthcare is assuming the printed price is the real price. It usually isn't. The cash or self-pay price is often a fraction of the sticker, and you just have to ask for it. I wrote about why that gap exists, and how to negotiate a bill down yourself.

This layer costs you nothing but the willingness to ask. It's the highest return move in the whole net.

Layer three: a way to cover the big stuff

Layers one and two handle the small and medium bumps. But a true catastrophe, a long hospital stay, a major surgery, can blow past any emergency fund. That's what layer three is for.

For a lot of families, that's insurance. For a lot of other families, health sharing fills this slot at a lower monthly cost, where the community funds the big eligible bills after the advocates negotiate them down. The point isn't which one you pick. The point is that you consciously have something in this slot, instead of hoping nothing big ever happens.

Why layers beat one big product

When you lean on a single product, its gaps become your gaps. High deductible? That's on you. Denied claim? On you. But when you've got layers, one weak spot doesn't sink you. The emergency fund covers what the cash price doesn't, the cash price shrinks what the big coverage sees, and the big coverage catches what would've been a catastrophe.

That's resilience. It's boring, and boring is exactly what you want when you're sick and stressed.

The takeaway

Stop looking for the one perfect plan that solves everything. Build the net instead: an emergency fund you can reach, the habit of asking for the cash price, and a real plan for the big stuff. Start with whichever layer you're missing. Each one you add makes the whole thing stronger, and none of them require you to have it all figured out today.

What's the first layer to build?

A real emergency fund, even a first $1,000. It turns a crisis into an inconvenience. If you use health sharing, this is where your $500 event commitment lives. If you're on insurance, it's what covers the deductible before the plan helps. Start with the first $1,000.

Which layer has the highest return?

Knowing the cash price. The most expensive mistake in American healthcare is assuming the printed price is the real price. The cash price is often a fraction of the sticker, and it costs you nothing but the willingness to ask. Here's how.

Do I need insurance or health sharing for layer three?

You need something in that slot. A long hospital stay or major surgery can blow past any emergency fund. For a lot of families that's insurance. For others, health sharing fills it at a lower monthly cost. The point is choosing consciously instead of hoping nothing big happens.

item.title: What If the Crowd Doesn't Fund Your Bill?
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: Health sharing has no legal guarantee, but a strong track record: 53,877 bills funded. Why bills get denied, and how to make the worst case survivable.
item.content:encoded:
In short: Yes, the crowd can decline a bill. There's no legal guarantee, ever. But most declines happen because the bill fell outside the written guidelines: something not eligible, a pre-existing waiting period not met, or incomplete paperwork. Read the rules first, keep your $500 plus a small emergency fund, and use the appeal process. Then the worst case is a bump, not a disaster.

This is the question I respect the most, because it's the one a careful person actually loses sleep over. Everybody selling health sharing wants to talk about the wins. I'd rather talk about the worst case with you first, because if the worst case is survivable, the rest of the decision gets easy. So let's stare at it straight.

The honest truth up front

Health sharing is not insurance. There is no legal contract that guarantees your bill gets paid. That's not fine print, that's the core of the model, and anyone who tells you otherwise is not being straight with you. When you join, you're joining a community that agrees to share eligible costs, not buying a legal promise.

I say this in every post that touches the money, and I mean it every time.

So how often does the crowd actually come through?

Here's the other half, and it matters just as much. The track record is strong and public. The CrowdHealth community, the service I use, has funded 53,877 bills, including single bills over $600,000. Complete, eligible submissions get funded in about a week on average. So while there's no legal guarantee, there's a long, real history of the crowd showing up. I dug into that trust question.

Strong history is not the same as an ironclad promise. Both things are true, and a smart person holds both.

Why bills actually get denied

Most of the time a bill doesn't get funded, it's not a mystery or a betrayal. It's because it fell outside the guidelines everyone agreed to. The usual reasons:

  • It was for something explicitly not eligible, like cosmetic work or certain pre-existing situations.
  • The waiting rules for a pre-existing condition weren't met yet.
  • The paperwork was incomplete, so it stalled until it got fixed.

The lesson is boring but powerful: read the guidelines before you join, and you avoid almost all of the surprises. The denials that shock people are usually things the guidelines said plainly all along.

How to make the worst case survivable

This is the part I actually do in my own life. You don't just trust and hope. You build a small backstop:

  • Keep your $500 event commitment liquid, always ready.
  • Keep a modest emergency fund on top of that, so a gap never wrecks you.
  • Know the guidelines so you're not submitting things that were never eligible.
  • Use the appeal process if something gets declined. It's not a dead end.

Do that, and even the bad scenario becomes a bump, not a catastrophe.

The takeaway

Could the crowd not fund a bill? Yes, and I won't pretend otherwise. There's no legal guarantee, ever. But the real risk is much smaller than the fear, because the track record is deep and most denials come from clear guideline rules you can read up front. Go in informed, keep a cushion, and the worst case is something you can handle. That's the honest deal, and honest is the only way I'll sell it.

How often does CrowdHealth not fund a bill?

The public track record is strong: 53,877 bills funded, 99.8 percent of them fully funded, including single bills over $600,000, with complete eligible submissions funded in about a week on average. Declines mostly come from clear guideline rules you can read up front, not from mystery.

Can I appeal if my bill is declined?

Yes. The appeal process is not a dead end. Often the fix is completing paperwork or documenting that the event was eligible. Keep every piece of paper from day one.

How do I protect myself against a declined bill?

Keep your $500 event commitment liquid, keep a modest emergency fund on top of it, know the guidelines so you never submit something that was never eligible, and appeal if needed. Do that and a gap never wrecks you. Start with the first $1,000.

item.title: High-Deductible Plan vs. Health Sharing: The Head-to-Head

item.description: High-deductible plan vs. health sharing, head to head: monthly cost, what happens at a health event, a real-year example, and where the insurance plan wins.
item.content:encoded:
In short: If you're healthy and already on a high-deductible plan to keep costs down, health sharing is usually the same bet made better: a lower monthly number ($60 per person plus a modest crowd contribution) and a $500 step per event instead of a $7,000 to $15,000 wall. The trade is giving up the legal guarantee and the hard out-of-pocket maximum.

A lot of responsible families end up on a high-deductible health plan because it has the lowest monthly bill on the menu. If that's you, you're already comfortable carrying some risk to keep your monthly cost down. That's exactly the mindset health sharing is built for. So let's put them side by side and do the actual math, no spin.

What each one costs you monthly

With a high-deductible plan, you pay a premium every month, and for a family that's often several hundred to over a thousand dollars, even before anyone gets sick. With health sharing through CrowdHealth, the service I use, you pay a flat $60 per person per month, plus a modest monthly contribution to the crowd. For most healthy families, the health sharing monthly number lands lower. I broke down the real monthly math.

So round one, monthly cost, usually goes to health sharing for a healthy family.

What happens when something goes wrong

This is where people get fooled by the word "coverage."

On a high-deductible plan, when a health event hits, you pay the full cost yourself until you reach your deductible, which is often $7,000 to $15,000 for a family. Only after you climb that wall does the plan start paying. You've been paying premiums the whole time, and you still eat the first several thousand dollars.

On health sharing, you pay $500 for the event, and the community funds the rest of the eligible bill after the advocates negotiate it down. No annual wall to climb first.

The math on a real year

Say a family has one solid health event, a $6,000 bill after discounts.

  • Health sharing: the flat fees for the year, plus $500 for the event. A dramatically smaller total.

Where the high-deductible plan wins

I promised no spin, so here it is. The high-deductible plan is real insurance, which means a legal guarantee and a hard yearly out-of-pocket maximum. Health sharing has neither, because it is not insurance. If you have a chronic condition, take costly ongoing medication, or simply cannot stomach any uncertainty, the guarantee is worth paying for. The takeaway

If you're healthy and already chose a high-deductible plan to keep costs down, health sharing is usually the same bet made better. Lower monthly cost, and a $500 step instead of a five-figure wall when something happens. The trade is giving up the legal guarantee. For a lot of us, that trade is clearly worth it. For some, it isn't. Now you can tell which one you are.

Often several hundred to over a thousand dollars a month in premiums, with a family deductible of $7,000 to $15,000 behind it. When a health event hits, you pay the full cost yourself until you reach that deductible, even though you've been paying premiums the whole time.

It's real insurance: a legal guarantee that covered claims get paid and a hard yearly out-of-pocket maximum. It also lets you open an HSA. If you have a chronic condition, take costly ongoing medication, or can't stomach uncertainty, that guarantee is worth paying for.
